bestFor: Turning a broad research question into a clear, answerable brief.
Building a report or recommendation from evidence instead of guesses.
Checking a draft for weak claims, missing sources, and unfinished work.

startHere.why: Use this front door when you know the outcome you want but are not sure which research, planning, writing, or review skill should handle it.

quickStarts.prompt: Research this question and build a concise, evidence-backed brief: [question]. Explain what is known, what is uncertain, and which sources support the answer.
Turn this request into a practical knowledge-work plan: [request]. Define the audience, scope, sources, deliverables, and checks before starting.
Review this draft for unsupported claims, missing evidence, unclear reasoning, and incomplete requirements. Show me the important fixes first: [draft].

workflow.title: Frame the job
workflow.instruction: Define the decision, reader, scope, source of truth, constraints, and signs of success.

workflow.title: Make the plan
workflow.instruction: Turn the frame into research, analysis, writing, and verification steps.

workflow.title: Research and test claims
workflow.instruction: Gather appropriate sources and check the important claims before drafting conclusions.

workflow.title: Draft from the evidence
workflow.instruction: Write the deliverable from the checked facts, with uncertainty and limitations made visible.

workflow.title: Review and finish
workflow.instruction: Check requirements and evidence, then package the result with a clear handoff.

skillPaths.need: You need to define the question before researching
skillPaths.why: It turns a loose request into a bounded job.

skillPaths.need: You need current or disputed facts
skillPaths.why: It organizes a source-first investigation.

skillPaths.need: You already have a draft and need a serious review
skillPaths.why: It checks the draft against requirements and evidence.

skillPaths.need: You received feedback and need to decide what to change
skillPaths.why: It checks each finding before revising the work.

workedExample.title: From a broad market question to a decision brief
workedExample.situation: A team needs to understand whether a new service is worth testing, but the original request is too broad.
steps: Frame the decision, intended reader, time window, and acceptable evidence.
Plan the research questions and prioritize primary or authoritative sources.
Test the main claims before writing the recommendation.
Draft the brief, disclose uncertainty, and verify every required section.
workedExample.result: A useful result is a short decision brief with traceable sources, clear uncertainty, and a recommendation tied to the evidence.

tips: Name the reader and the decision they need to make.
Give a time window when facts may have changed.
Separate must-answer questions from interesting side questions.
Share the source material you already trust.
boundaries: It does not make weak evidence stronger. It should mark gaps and uncertainty.
It does not publish, send, buy, or approve anything unless you separately authorize that action.
Simple lookups may not need the full workflow.
successSignals: The result answers the original question for the intended reader.
Important claims can be traced to appropriate sources.
Unknowns, limitations, and unfinished items are stated plainly.

bestFor: Turning a fuzzy idea into a result that can be checked.
Pressure-testing a plan before spending time or money.
Breaking an approved brief into small, verifiable pieces of work.
Carrying a project from clarification through delivery.

startHere.why: Start here when you want one guided path from an unclear goal to a verified result. It chooses the narrower skills as the work becomes clear.

quickStarts.prompt: Run Outcome Engine on this idea: [idea]. Help me define the real outcome, resolve the important decisions, and stop before implementation if approval is needed.
Turn these settled notes into an execution-ready outcome brief. Keep the decisions already made and identify only genuine gaps: [notes].
Break this approved outcome into small action slices with dependencies, proof for each slice, and a clear definition of done: [outcome].

workflow.title: Resolve the goal
workflow.instruction: Ask only the consequential questions needed to understand the desired result and constraints.

workflow.title: Write the outcome brief
workflow.instruction: Turn settled context into a durable brief with scope, deliverables, boundaries, and proof.

workflow.title: Slice the work
workflow.instruction: Create small end-to-end units that can be completed and checked independently.

workflow.title: Deliver with evidence
workflow.instruction: Complete each approved slice through a check, change, and verify loop.

workflow.title: Improve the system
workflow.instruction: After the outcome is delivered, examine structural friction only when that review is useful.

skillPaths.need: The idea is still unclear
skillPaths.why: It resolves one important decision at a time.

skillPaths.need: The conversation is settled but not documented
skillPaths.why: It turns context into a durable handoff.

skillPaths.need: The work is too large to execute safely
skillPaths.why: It creates smaller results with their own checks.

skillPaths.need: The plan is approved and ready to implement
skillPaths.why: It keeps progress tied to observable changes.

workedExample.title: From a rough workshop idea to a ready plan
workedExample.situation: A creator wants to offer a workshop but has not settled the audience, promise, format, or proof of demand.
steps: Clarify the audience, desired change, constraints, and no-go areas.
Create a brief for the workshop test rather than the entire future program.
Split the test into offer, landing copy, outreach draft, and evidence review.
Complete and verify each approved slice before calling the test ready.
workedExample.result: A useful result is a bounded workshop test with an approved brief, practical work units, and clear evidence for readiness.

tips: Describe the change you want, not only the artifact you want produced.
State what must remain unchanged.
Decide what evidence would make you confident enough to stop.
Use the full coordinator for multi-stage work and a specialist for one clear stage.
boundaries: It does not treat a plan, checklist, or draft as proof that the outcome exists.
It pauses for approval when a decision or action would materially expand the agreed scope.
It does not grant permission to publish, send messages, purchase, or delete.
successSignals: The desired result and definition of done are explicit.
Each action slice produces something observable and checkable.
Required work is complete or clearly marked unresolved.

bestFor: Running an important task through an evidence-gated refinement loop.
Reviewing proposed lessons before they influence later work.
Auditing whether a learning loop is improving results or adding noise.

startHere.why: Use this only when you explicitly want ProofLoop to wrap a task. It keeps execution bounded and puts candidate lessons into review instead of treating them as trusted memory.

quickStarts.prompt: Use ProofLoop to complete this task: [task]. Define the verifier, attempt limit, stop conditions, and evidence required before starting.
Review these ProofLoop candidate lessons. Approve only lessons that are supported, safe, reusable, and narrow enough: [candidates].
Audit whether ProofLoop is helping on these runs. Compare outcomes, verifier quality, memory usefulness, failures, cost, and drift: [run records].

workflow.title: Define the bounded run
workflow.instruction: Set the task, evidence standard, maximum attempts, authority, and stop conditions.

workflow.title: Execute and judge
workflow.instruction: Produce a candidate result, judge it against the stated verifier, and refine only within the attempt limit.

workflow.title: Verify the outcome
workflow.instruction: Check the final result with fresh evidence and record failures without hiding them.

workflow.title: Quarantine lessons
workflow.instruction: Keep proposed learning separate until a person or authorized review approves it.

workflow.title: Audit over time
workflow.instruction: Use read-only evidence to decide whether the loop is improving quality without harmful drift.

skillPaths.need: You want to wrap one task in the protocol
skillPaths.why: It runs the bounded writer, judge, execution, and verification process.

skillPaths.need: You need to approve, reject, expire, or narrow a lesson
skillPaths.why: It governs candidate memory instead of trusting it automatically.

skillPaths.need: You want to know whether the system is helping
skillPaths.why: It performs a read-only effectiveness and safety review.

workedExample.title: Improving a recurring briefing task without uncontrolled learning
workedExample.situation: A team repeats the same briefing task and wants the process to improve without silently changing its rules.
steps: Define the briefing requirements, verifier, attempt limit, and stop conditions.
Run one briefing through the bounded protocol and preserve the evidence.
Record proposed lessons as candidates rather than active instructions.
Review the candidates and later audit whether approved lessons improved results.
workedExample.result: A useful result is a verified briefing plus a reviewable learning record that cannot silently replace the source instructions.

tips: Give the verifier concrete requirements, not a vague quality score.
Keep attempt limits small enough to prevent endless refinement.
Treat candidate lessons as suggestions until reviewed.
Preserve failed runs because they are part of the evidence.
boundaries: ProofLoop is explicit-only. Generic improvement requests should not trigger it.
It does not expand the authority of the wrapped task.
Candidate lessons do not become trusted instructions without the required review.
An audit is read-only and does not repair the system.
successSignals: The run has a finite attempt limit and a specific verifier.
The final result includes evidence and honest failure records.
Learning candidates remain governed, reviewable, and reversible.

bestFor: Choosing the right kind of writing help before changing a draft.
Drafting or rewriting serious prose for a specific reader and purpose.
Reviewing text without rewriting it.
Checking whether factual claims are supported and properly qualified.

startHere.why: Start here when the request could mean drafting, rewriting, review, claim checking, or final cleanup. It picks the smallest intervention that matches your intent.

quickStarts.prompt: Write this for [reader] so they can [decision or action]. Use this evidence and preserve these constraints: [material].
Review this draft without rewriting it. Identify unclear intent, generic language, unsupported claims, and the highest-value fixes: [draft].
Check the claim boundaries in this draft. Separate supported facts, reasonable inferences, unsupported claims, and statements that need current verification: [draft].

workflow.title: Name the writing job
workflow.instruction: Identify the reader, purpose, desired response, source material, and whether the request is draft, rewrite, review, or claim check.

workflow.title: Build the intent
workflow.instruction: Shape the hierarchy and argument around what the reader needs to understand or do.

workflow.title: Draft or rewrite
workflow.instruction: Produce clear prose while preserving approved meaning, evidence, and voice.

workflow.title: Check claims
workflow.instruction: Label unsupported facts, inference, uncertainty, and verification needs before publication.

workflow.title: Run the final prose check
workflow.instruction: Remove filler, repetition, vague phrasing, and mechanical problems without changing the meaning.

skillPaths.need: You are not sure what kind of writing help is needed
skillPaths.why: It routes the request before text is changed.

skillPaths.need: The document lacks a clear reader or argument
skillPaths.why: It creates the communication structure first.

skillPaths.need: You need drafting, rewriting, or final prose cleanup
skillPaths.why: It produces or refines the actual prose.

skillPaths.need: The draft contains factual or time-sensitive claims
skillPaths.why: It separates evidence from inference and unsupported language.

workedExample.title: Turning rough product notes into credible launch copy
workedExample.situation: A team has accurate product notes, but the first draft is generic and makes claims the evidence does not support.
steps: Define the intended reader, the action they should take, and the approved facts.
Build a message hierarchy around the reader's problem and the product's supported value.
Draft the copy in the requested voice.
Check every factual claim and remove or qualify unsupported language.
workedExample.result: A useful result is clear launch copy that sounds intentional, preserves the source meaning, and makes only supportable claims.

tips: Say whether you want a draft, a rewrite, or comments only.
Name the audience and the action the text should support.
Provide source material for factual claims.
List phrases, tone habits, or meaning that must be preserved.
boundaries: A detect-only review should not silently rewrite your text.
The plugin cannot verify a claim without an appropriate source or access to current evidence.
Clear prose cannot repair a weak strategy or missing facts by itself.
successSignals: The writing has a clear reader, purpose, and information order.
Claims are supported, qualified, or marked for verification.
The final text keeps the intended meaning and contains no filler.

bestFor: Choosing the right installed plugin or skill for a request.
Inventorying capabilities on one host without changing them.
Finding overlap, unclear ownership, or stale plugin records.
Installing, releasing, and proving a plugin when explicitly requested.

startHere.why: Use the router when you need the correct capability but do not already know its name. It should select the narrowest owner before any install or change.

quickStarts.prompt: Choose the best installed plugin or skill for this request: [request]. Explain the match, any missing capability, and whether the task requires a change.
Create a read-only inventory of the plugins and skills visible on this host. Separate source files, installed state, and capabilities proven in a fresh task.
Audit these skills for overlap and unclear ownership without changing anything. Recommend one primary route and explicit fallbacks: [skills or plugins].

workflow.title: Identify the host and goal
workflow.instruction: Name the active host, requested outcome, and whether this is routing, inventory, audit, install, creation, or release.

workflow.title: Inspect current state
workflow.instruction: Read the authoritative records and distinguish source, cache, enabled listing, and fresh-task visibility.

workflow.title: Choose or repair ownership
workflow.instruction: Route the request, inspect overlap, or update portfolio ownership only within the approved scope.

workflow.title: Make the authorized change
workflow.instruction: Install, create, or release only when the user asked for that state change.

workflow.title: Prove discovery and parity
workflow.instruction: Verify release evidence, installed parity, and fresh-task discovery for the changed plugin.

skillPaths.need: You need the best existing capability
skillPaths.why: It resolves ownership before work starts.

skillPaths.need: You need a read-only map of what exists
skillPaths.why: It separates files from installed and discoverable state.

skillPaths.need: Two skills seem to do the same job
skillPaths.why: It compares scope and recommends clearer ownership.

skillPaths.need: A plugin changed and needs proof
skillPaths.why: It checks the release chain rather than trusting filesystem presence.

workedExample.title: Finding the right capability before installing another plugin
workedExample.situation: A user wants help with a recurring research task and assumes a new plugin is required.
steps: Route the request against the capabilities already visible on the active host.
Inventory the likely owners and distinguish installed state from source files.
Audit overlap if several skills appear to fit.
Recommend the primary route, and install something new only if a real gap remains and approval is given.
workedExample.result: A useful result is one clear primary capability, a reason it fits, and evidence for any claimed installation or discovery state.

tips: Name the host because availability can differ between hosts.
Say whether you want a read-only answer or an actual install or release.
Describe the outcome, not only the tool name you remember.
Ask for fresh-task proof when discovery matters.
boundaries: Technical access does not authorize installation, deletion, publishing, or portfolio changes.
A source folder does not prove a plugin is installed or visible in a new task.
The plugin should not create a new capability when an existing owner already fits.
successSignals: The chosen capability has a clear reason and owner.
Source, installed, enabled, and fresh-task states are not confused.
Any changed plugin has direct parity and discovery evidence.

bestFor: Turning an internal-tool idea into a governed application plan.
Building or changing an internal app with explicit owners and policies.
Explaining a blocked application decision in plain language.
Operating and releasing an app through defined lifecycle controls.

startHere.why: Start with the coordinator when the request spans idea, policy, build, release, or operations. It routes the job to the correct lifecycle stage.

quickStarts.prompt: Help me turn this internal-tool idea into a safe application brief: [idea]. Identify users, data, decisions, owners, policies, and risks before building.
Check whether this Citizen Forge application is ready to release. Verify the registered owner, policy decisions, tests, operating plan, and unresolved blockers: [app details].
Explain why this application action was blocked in plain language. Name the rule, the evidence, the safe next step, and who must approve it: [event].

workflow.title: Define the idea
workflow.instruction: Clarify the users, problem, desired decision or action, data involved, and measurable value.

workflow.title: Register ownership and policy
workflow.instruction: Record the application, accountable owner, data boundaries, permissions, and lifecycle controls.

workflow.title: Build the bounded application
workflow.instruction: Implement only the approved capabilities and deterministic policy behavior.

workflow.title: Check and release
workflow.instruction: Verify readiness, document limits, and release only with the required approvals.

workflow.title: Operate and change safely
workflow.instruction: Triage issues, explain policy decisions, and route material changes back through review.

skillPaths.need: You have an app idea but no safe brief
skillPaths.why: It defines the user, value, data, and decision boundary.

skillPaths.need: The app needs an owner and registry record
skillPaths.why: It creates accountable lifecycle ownership.

skillPaths.need: You need to implement the approved application
skillPaths.why: It builds within the agreed policy and scope.

skillPaths.need: A user needs to understand a blocked action
skillPaths.why: It translates policy evidence into a useful explanation.

workedExample.title: Building an internal request tracker
workedExample.situation: A small team wants an app that collects requests, assigns owners, and shows status without exposing restricted information.
steps: Define who submits, who approves, which fields are sensitive, and what success means.
Register the owner and policy for viewing, editing, and escalating requests.
Build the approved form, status view, and deterministic access checks.
Verify the policy paths and operating plan before release.
workedExample.result: A useful result is an owned, registered internal app whose allowed actions, blocked actions, and operating responsibilities are clear.

tips: Start with one real internal decision or workflow.
Name the accountable owner before building.
List sensitive data and forbidden actions explicitly.
Describe the normal operating and support process, not only the first release.
boundaries: It does not replace security, privacy, legal, or compliance review where those are required.
It should not provision access or release an app without the required authority.
A prototype is not automatically a governed production application.
successSignals: The app has a named owner, registered purpose, and explicit policies.
Allowed and blocked actions behave predictably.
Release and ongoing operation have evidence and clear responsibilities.

bestFor: Designing a reusable agent system instead of a one-off prompt.
Defining authority, evidence, stops, handoffs, and failure behavior.
Auditing an agent workflow before it runs.
Choosing between a goal, loop, handoff, or broader agent architecture.

startHere.why: Use the router when you know the outcome but not the right agent pattern. It decides whether the job needs a single agent, loop, goal, handoff, or audit.

quickStarts.prompt: Design a bounded agent system for this outcome: [outcome]. Define ownership, authority, inputs, outputs, evidence, stops, failures, and handoffs.
Audit this agent system before it runs. Find unclear authority, missing evidence, unsafe handoffs, endless-loop risks, and weak completion rules: [system].
Route this reusable agent request to the smallest suitable architecture. Explain whether it needs an agent, goal, loop, handoff, or another pattern: [request].

workflow.title: Choose the pattern
workflow.instruction: Classify the outcome and select the smallest agent architecture that can own it safely.

workflow.title: Define the contract
workflow.instruction: Specify inputs, outputs, authority, evidence, stop conditions, failure behavior, and human approvals.

workflow.title: Add orchestration only when needed
workflow.instruction: Use goals or loops for sustained work and keep each one bounded by durable state and proof.

workflow.title: Prepare host handoffs
workflow.instruction: When work moves between environments, preserve the contract and translate host-specific execution details.

workflow.title: Audit the whole system
workflow.instruction: Check the architecture, authority, evidence, stops, and failure paths before relying on it.

skillPaths.need: You need the basic reusable agent contract
skillPaths.why: It defines the system's job, authority, evidence, and stops.

skillPaths.need: You need a bounded goal that persists
skillPaths.why: It wraps sustained work in explicit completion rules.

skillPaths.need: You need repeating work with checkpoints
skillPaths.why: It designs the loop and its durable state.

skillPaths.need: You need an independent safety and completeness check
skillPaths.why: It reviews the whole system before execution.

workedExample.title: Designing a weekly research agent
workedExample.situation: A team wants a recurring agent that watches a topic and produces a short update only when meaningful changes occur.
steps: Choose a bounded loop rather than an always-on general agent.
Define sources, the meaning of a material change, the report format, and no-op behavior.
Set the schedule, durable checkpoint, evidence requirements, and stop conditions.
Audit authority and failure handling before activation.
workedExample.result: A useful result is a reusable agent contract that knows what to inspect, when to report, when to do nothing, and when to stop.

tips: Define the outcome before choosing the architecture.
Make no-op behavior explicit for recurring systems.
State which actions need human approval.
Describe failures and recovery before the first run.
boundaries: It does not grant an agent more authority than the user supplied.
It does not make an unbounded task safe merely by adding more agents.
Host-specific setup may require a dedicated tool or connector.
Advisory skills do not execute changes unless the request authorizes them.
successSignals: Every component has one clear job and owner.
Evidence, approval, stop, and failure rules are explicit.
The system can be resumed or audited without relying on hidden chat context.

bestFor: Turning a video brief into a complete production plan.
Choosing the right video format and production path.
Building captions, graphics, and prompts for a video.
Checking a finished render before delivery.

startHere.why: Start here with the audience, message, available media, format, and deadline. It routes the job to the smallest suitable production workflow.

quickStarts.prompt: Route this video brief into a complete production plan: [brief]. Recommend the format, workflow, required media, review points, and delivery checks.
Turn this product launch into a video workflow. Define the audience, core promise, story beats, visuals, captions, production method, and approval points: [launch details].
Run delivery quality control on this rendered video. Check picture, audio, captions, timing, safe areas, file properties, and the original brief: [video or path].

workflow.title: Route the brief
workflow.instruction: Choose the production pattern from the message, audience, media, runtime, platform, and available tools.

workflow.title: Build the production prompt
workflow.instruction: Translate the approved idea into scenes, timing, visual direction, audio, text, and constraints.

workflow.title: Produce the right format
workflow.instruction: Use the specialist for the chosen format and keep source media use within its approved rights and role.

workflow.title: Add communication layers
workflow.instruction: Create readable captions and purposeful graphic overlays when the video needs them.

workflow.title: Verify delivery
workflow.instruction: Inspect the actual render against the brief and technical delivery requirements.

skillPaths.need: You need a clear narrated explainer
skillPaths.why: It structures an explanation without requiring an on-camera presenter.

skillPaths.need: You need a product launch story
skillPaths.why: It maps the product promise into a launch-focused sequence.

skillPaths.need: You need motion-led graphics
skillPaths.why: It handles animation-first visual communication.

skillPaths.need: You need a website turned into video
skillPaths.why: It plans capture and presentation from an existing web surface.

skillPaths.need: You need final render checks
skillPaths.why: It verifies the delivered file rather than the production plan.

workedExample.title: A short launch explainer
workedExample.situation: A product team has approved messaging, interface captures, and a 45-second target but no production structure.
steps: Route the brief to a product-launch workflow.
Turn the approved promise into timed scenes and define each media source.
Build the video with readable captions and restrained overlays.
Render the candidate and inspect picture, audio, timing, and brief alignment.
workedExample.result: A useful result is a delivery-ready video whose story, media, captions, and technical properties match the approved brief.

tips: Give the target platform, aspect ratio, runtime, and audience.
Separate approved media from media that still needs rights clearance.
Write one communication goal for each scene.
Review a rendered file, not only the timeline or source code.
boundaries: The plugin does not supply rights to images, music, footage, logos, or voices.
Generation and rendering may require separate media or runtime tools.
Publishing or uploading needs separate approval.
A production plan is not proof that a final video rendered correctly.
successSignals: The video has one clear audience and message.
Every scene, asset, and caption has a defined role.
The final render passes both brief and technical delivery checks.

bestFor: Building a web product from an approved brief.
Redesigning an existing interface while preserving its real behavior.
Turning an image or screenshot into a working web surface.
Verifying the most important user flows in a browser.
Locking a load-bearing visual hero before feature expansion.

startHere.why: Use the router when the job could be a new build, redesign, image implementation, or verification task. It chooses one visual authority and hands likeness-dependent hero work to the hidden visual-fidelity-gate specialist before secondary features.

quickStarts.prompt: Route and build this web product from the brief: [brief]. Preserve the named constraints, choose one visual direction, implement the core flows, and verify them in a browser.
Redesign this existing interface without changing its product behavior: [project or URL]. First map the current flows, then improve the visual system and verify the result.
Turn this screenshot into a working responsive web surface: [image]. Reconstruct the visual rules, use real structure, and verify mobile and desktop behavior.

workflow.title: Route the web job
workflow.instruction: Identify whether this is a new build, redesign, image-to-code task, or verification-only request.

workflow.title: Choose the visual authority
workflow.instruction: Set one design constitution that governs type, color, spacing, components, motion, and responsive behavior.

workflow.title: Implement the product
workflow.instruction: Build the requested surface and preserve current behavior when the job is a redesign.

workflow.title: Lock the representative hero
workflow.instruction: For likeness-dependent or picture-led work, validate the source-bound hero separately before expanding secondary features.

workflow.title: Complete the requested output
workflow.instruction: Check that the implementation is not a partial mockup and that every approved requirement has a terminal result.

workflow.title: Verify real flows
workflow.instruction: Run the important acceptance paths and inspect the rendered product at relevant viewport sizes.

skillPaths.need: You are redesigning an existing project
skillPaths.why: It starts from the current product and protects working behavior.

skillPaths.need: You are building from a visual reference
skillPaths.why: It translates the reference into responsive structure and styles.

skillPaths.need: You need a new visual frontend direction
skillPaths.why: It supports intentional, high-quality frontend visual design.

skillPaths.need: You need fast browser-level implementation and QA
skillPaths.why: It combines headless product work with verification.

skillPaths.need: You need to prove a critical user path
skillPaths.why: It tests the outcome from the user's point of view.

skillPaths.need: The first-glance hero must match a visual reference
skillPaths.why: It locks the target, reviews the representative hero independently, and stops below the visual threshold.

workedExample.title: Redesigning a working directory
workedExample.situation: A directory already has good content and filters, but visitors must click twice to reach an item page and the detail pages are too thin.
steps: Map the current routes, filters, design tokens, and mobile behavior.
Choose the existing design system as the visual authority.
Replace selector rows with direct links and expand the detail template.
Run build checks and browser tests for navigation, focus, responsive layout, and content.
workedExample.result: A useful result is a working redesign that keeps the product's identity, shortens the main path, and passes the agreed browser flows.

tips: Provide the repository or live URL and name the source of truth.
List behavior that must not change.
Define the top three user flows before styling.
Give exact viewport sizes when responsive details matter.
boundaries: A screenshot does not reveal hidden product logic or data rules.
A local build does not prove the public deployment is current.
Deployment, domains, credentials, and paid services may require separate tools and approval.
A redesign should not silently rewrite product behavior.
successSignals: The main user flows work in the rendered product.
The visual system is consistent across routes and viewport sizes.
Accessibility, error states, and completion checks are part of the result.

bestFor: Choosing a verified prompt workflow for a specific model.
Building production prompts with explicit inputs, outputs, and checks.
Auditing a prompt before moving it to another model.
Designing a representative benchmark for prompt decisions.

startHere.why: Start here when model choice or prompt format is part of the problem. It routes to a model-specific workflow only when the evidence supports that route.

quickStarts.prompt: Route this prompt job to the right verified model workflow: [job]. State the model assumptions, required inputs, output contract, and checks.
Audit this prompt before migrating it from [source model] to [target model]. Identify incompatible instructions, missing controls, and a safe test plan: [prompt].
Design a small representative benchmark for this production prompt. Include normal cases, edge cases, scoring rules, and a decision threshold: [prompt and job].

workflow.title: Define the prompt job
workflow.instruction: Name the model, task, inputs, required output, constraints, tools, and evidence for success.

workflow.title: Use the verified model workflow
workflow.instruction: Build the prompt with the specialist whose model contract matches the confirmed target.

workflow.title: Audit migration risks
workflow.instruction: When changing models, inspect assumptions and behavior instead of renaming the model in place.

workflow.title: Build a representative test
workflow.instruction: Create cases and scoring that reflect the real production task.

workflow.title: Choose from measured evidence
workflow.instruction: Compare results and revise the prompt or model route only when the benchmark justifies it.

skillPaths.need: You have a verified GPT-5.6 prompt job
skillPaths.why: It applies the production contract for that model family.

skillPaths.need: You have a verified GPT-5.4 prompt job
skillPaths.why: It uses the matching production prompt workflow.

skillPaths.need: You have a Fable 5 prompt job
skillPaths.why: It composes the appropriate Fable production structure.

skillPaths.need: You are moving a prompt between models
skillPaths.why: It finds assumptions that may not transfer.

skillPaths.need: You need evidence for a prompt decision
skillPaths.why: It creates representative cases and scoring.

workedExample.title: Moving a production extraction prompt
workedExample.situation: A team wants to move a working extraction prompt to another model without losing schema compliance or evidence handling.
steps: Define the input types, output schema, error behavior, and current success rate evidence.
Audit the original prompt for model-specific assumptions.
Build the target-model version with the verified specialist.
Run both prompts on representative normal and edge cases before choosing.
workedExample.result: A useful result is a target prompt with an explicit contract and measured evidence that supports or rejects the migration.

tips: Name the exact model and interface when known.
Provide representative inputs, including hard cases.
Define the output schema and failure behavior before prompt wording.
Compare measured outputs, not confidence in the prose.
boundaries: Model behavior and interfaces can change, so unstable claims need current verification.
A polished prompt is not evidence that it performs well.
The plugin does not provide model access, credentials, or usage budget.
Do not transfer host-specific paths or tools into another environment without adaptation.
successSignals: The prompt names its inputs, outputs, constraints, and failure behavior.
The chosen route matches a verified model contract.

Prove one manual run before adding a schedule.

Repeated unchanged state is a diagnosis signal, not proof of progress.

steps: Create and approve a brief with the source hierarchy and exact definition of done.
Prepare finite workstreams and define evidence for each deliverable.

workedExample.result: A useful result is a complete documentation system whose artifacts, source fidelity, checks, and unresolved items are independently inspectable.

tips: Use the explicit Gauntlet name so it cannot trigger accidentally.
Set resource limits and deliverables before worker activity.
Keep evidence compact and tied to the final requirements.
